title: Query Optimizer Handbook: From SQL to Execution Plan
summary: Quick revision notes on how a database turns SQL into a plan: parsing and rewriting, cost-based choices driven by statistics, join algorithms, scan types, and how to read an execution plan.

chapters.title: Query Pipeline and Optimizer Mental Model
points: Pipeline stages in order: parse (syntax check, build parse tree) → analyze/bind (resolve tables, columns, types, permissions) → rewrite (views expanded, subqueries flattened, constants folded) → plan/optimize → execute
SQL is declarative: you state what rows you want and the optimizer picks how, so the same query can run with very different plans as data changes
Rewriting is rule-based and cost-free: expand views, flatten IN/EXISTS subqueries into joins, fold constants, push predicates down before the planner runs
The planner enumerates candidate plans (access paths, join order, join methods), estimates the cost of each and keeps the cheapest; it does not guarantee the truly fastest one
Prepared statements and plan caches reuse one plan, which can go wrong when parameter values have very different selectivity (parameter sniffing / generic plan problem)

chapters.title: Cost-Based Optimization, Statistics and Selectivity
points: Cost model: total cost = estimated I/O + CPU work, in abstract units (e.g. PostgreSQL seq_page_cost=1.0, random_page_cost=4.0 by default); costs compare plans, they are not milliseconds
Statistics gathered by ANALYZE / UPDATE STATISTICS: row count, page count, per-column distinct count, null fraction, most common values with frequencies, and histogram buckets
Selectivity = fraction of rows a predicate keeps (0 to 1); estimated rows = table rows × selectivity; for equality, selectivity ≈ 1 / distinct values unless the value is in the most-common list
Independent predicates multiply: sel(A AND B) = sel(A) × sel(B); this assumption breaks on correlated columns (city and zip) and underestimates rows by orders of magnitude

Stale statistics or skewed data cause bad row estimates, and a bad row estimate early in the plan compounds into the wrong join order and join method; fix with ANALYZE, extended/multi-column statistics, or a higher statistics target

chapters.title: Index Scans vs Sequential Scans
points: Sequential scan reads every page in order, cheap per page; index scan walks the B-tree then fetches each matching heap row with random I/O; index-only scan answers from the index alone if the visibility map shows pages are all-visible
Rule of thumb: the index wins when a predicate returns a small fraction of rows (roughly under 5-10%); above that, a seq scan is cheaper and the planner is right to choose it
Bitmap scan is the middle ground: build a bitmap of matching pages from the index, then read heap pages in physical order; used for medium selectivity and for combining several indexes with AND/OR

Index not used because: function or cast on the column (WHERE lower(email)=... needs an expression index), leading wildcard LIKE '%x', type mismatch, wrong column order in a composite index, or tiny table
A covering index (INCLUDE columns) allows an index-only scan; a composite index (a,b) serves filters on a or a+b but not b alone; low-cardinality columns rarely benefit from an index

chapters.title: Join Algorithms: Nested Loop vs Hash vs Merge
points: Nested loop: for each outer row, probe the inner side; cost ≈ outer rows × inner lookup cost; best when the outer side is small and the inner side has an index on the join key; the only method for non-equality joins without extra support

Hash join: build an in-memory hash table on the smaller input, then stream the larger input and probe it; equality joins only; no index or sort needed; if the build side exceeds work_mem/memory grant it spills to disk in batches and slows sharply
Merge join: both inputs sorted on the join key, then merged in one pass; equality (and range-ordered) joins; wins when inputs are already sorted by an index or ORDER BY, or are both very large

Choosing guide: small outer + indexed inner → nested loop; large unsorted equality join → hash; large pre-sorted inputs → merge; join order matters because the planner puts the smaller or more filtered input first

Classic trap: nested loop chosen because row estimate was 10 but actual was 1,000,000, causing a million index probes; fix the estimate (ANALYZE, extended stats) rather than forcing the join method with hints

chapters.title: Reading an Execution Plan
points: EXPLAIN shows the estimated plan without running; EXPLAIN ANALYZE (PostgreSQL) actually executes the query and adds real time and row counts, so wrap data-changing statements in a transaction and roll back; add BUFFERS to see page hits and reads
Read the tree from the innermost, most-indented node outward: leaf scans feed joins, joins feed sort/aggregate; each node shows cost=startup..total, rows=estimate, width=bytes per row
Compare estimated rows with actual rows on every node: a gap of 10x or more marks where the optimizer went wrong, and is the first thing to look for

Watch for red flags: Seq Scan on a large table with a selective filter, Rows Removed by Filter in the millions, Sort or Hash spilling to disk (Sort Method: external merge, Batches > 1), nested loop with huge loops count, and actual time multiplied by loops

Example fix flow: slow query → EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) → find the node with the largest actual time → check its estimate vs actual → ANALYZE or add an index or rewrite the predicate → re-run and compare

chapters.title: Optimizer Cheat Sheet
points: Pipeline: parse → bind → rewrite → plan → execute; the optimizer picks the cheapest estimated plan, not the guaranteed fastest
Selectivity = matching rows ÷ total rows; AND multiplies, OR adds minus overlap; refresh with ANALYZE after bulk loads
Scan choice: high selectivity (few rows) → index scan; medium → bitmap scan; most of the table → seq scan; index-only needs a covering index and a vacuumed table
Join choice: nested loop = small outer + indexed inner; hash = big equality join, watch memory spill; merge = pre-sorted inputs
Plan debugging checklist: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) → compare estimated vs actual rows → fix statistics first, then indexes, then rewrite the query; never rely on hints as the first fix
